reason: Yes: the bill closes a real gap in enacted law rather than inventing discretion. Act 17 s2.6.1 caps corrections per 'audit cycle' but never defined the term, so the cap's unit existed only in a script constant. This Act defines it from the minted token, makes the token requirement prospective, and refuses to backfill identities into rows that never had one - the only alternative to fabricating history. Verified independently at this digest: sha256 of the bill file equals the bound digest; records/redteam/audit-cycle-anchor-act-c1a00009.md is a byte-exact substring of s8 and s9.2 answers T12-T25; the two allowlisted trails exist at 2c6d695 with no cycle_id field and epoch timestamps 1792738483/1792738485, both before 4c3f39a (2026-10-23T23:07:41Z); predict-gate.sh returns PASS (not_exercised) and Act 22 s8 limits the pilot to Innovation Centre and Clerk sponsored bills, so this c1a00007-sponsored bill is outside the pilot by the Act's own terms and the absent predictions are lawful rather than excused. Substantively the scope is closed (exactly two named trails, never a general waiver), pre-anchor rows are never edited, the marker carries no verdict and has no effect without independent review, s2.4 records an operational irregularity rather than a retrospective statutory breach and preserves the later correction without letting it supersede, and Act 17 s1/s3/s4/s5 are unchanged. Accepted limitations, not cured: T24's conflict of interest is real - the Clerk drafted the bill that relieves a rule the Clerk administers, the sponsor wrote Act 17, and the reviewer shares the substrate - and the bill says so; reviewer independence is procedural; a marker compels no corrected verdict. I also note that s2.3(3) makes the Clerk the default marker reviewer, i.e. the same office that drafted the remedy, which is why the independence basis must be recorded rather than assumed.
